name: get the intended change approved before implementing it
about: The gate before any code, and this step's `gate` field is where that sentence goes: whoever writes this step into a plan writes it there by hand, in words about THIS job, because a definition cannot author one and a step left with an empty `gate` reads to every later reader as a step needing nobody. Write the summary IN YOUR OWN CHAT — that is what he reads — in the bullet format `sb presets design-gate` prints, then `sb block` with one short line naming what you are waiting for. Two sections, and they are this step's own names for them. FIRST, Scope & Objectives: the scope is yours to derive, what the work covers; the objectives are HIS, inferred from what he actually asked for and restated so nothing he wanted goes missing. SECOND, the Change Contract, bulletpointed and high-level only — no implementation detail, no jargon, nested where the nesting means something. Order it for READING and not for building: he goes top to bottom once, and should finish knowing what the change looks like at a high level, what behaviour changes and which modules are touched, with little context on this codebase. He answers approve, or rejects with changes. ON A REJECTION YOU REDO THE DESIGN WORK — re-derive the scope, re-infer the objectives, rebuild the contract — and then summarise and block again; editing the wording of a summary he rejected is answering a different question from the one he asked. Bump `tries` and put the step back to `open` each time round. When he approves, put the FULL approved text — both sections, entire — in the step's `output` field, by hand in the plan file, because that is what the PR comment dumps, and only then tick. Write it there as MARKDOWN-READY NESTING — two-space indents under `-` — rather than as the `-`/`---`/`-----` marker levels you wrote in chat, so the PR comment renders as the nested bullets he read. EMPTY THE `gate` FIELD as you tick: the answer it was holding the step for has arrived, and a gate left on a step that is already done is a defect `validate` reports and the board draws red — the approved text in `output` is the mark that the gate was reached and passed. This step comes BEFORE implementation and is an early root of the plan, whatever order it was added in — that is where naming it puts it. Obliges `review`, which is where the contract you got approved is checked against what was built. A trivially small change skips this with the reason in `why`: a behavioural contract for a typo is a block nobody wants.
